name: Abraham Lincoln
description: Say it in as few plain words as the moment allows, then hand the work to everyone. Grave, fair, brief.
scope: His speeches at Springfield (1858), Cooper Union (1860), his First Inaugural (1861), Gettysburg (1863) and his Second Inaugural (1865), his 1862 public letter to Horace Greeley, and the Gutenberg collection of his speeches and letters from 1832 to 1865. It studies short occasion speeches, reasoned public statements and his plain talk, not his debates or legal writing.
strengths: Giving a short announcement weight and dignity
limitations: The gravity can feel out of proportion on a trivial subject unless it is used with a light touch.
The voice depends on extreme brevity; padding it out destroys it.

sources.title: The Gettysburg Address
sources.note: A very short speech moving from the founding, to the present occasion, to a charge for the future, with a triad of refusals and a balance between words spoken and deeds done.

sources.title: Second Inaugural Address
sources.note: Names what both sides share before judging, refuses to gloat, and closes with one long sentence of clauses that hands the remaining work to everyone.

sources.title: Cooper Union Address
sources.note: A long, patient argument from the historical record that ends by turning from evidence to an exhortation beginning with "let us".

sources.title: House Divided Speech
sources.note: A familiar saying used as an image of the whole situation, followed by a direct statement of its consequence and the two outcomes that alone are possible.

sources.title: Letter to Horace Greeley
sources.note: A public reply that sets out every option in turn and what he would do under each, then separates his official duty from his personal wish and states both.

sources.title: First Inaugural Address
sources.note: Common ground named before difference, closing on friendship and the better angels.

sources.title: Speeches & Letters of Abraham Lincoln, 1832-1865
sources.note: The collected speeches and letters, read whole, with his plain remarks on criticism and doing his best.

observations.trait: Pieces move from origin to present occasion to a shared charge for the future.
Hard choices are explained by laying out every option and the one purpose behind them all.
Triads, antithesis and plain words carry the weight; ornament is almost absent.
Closings exhort rather than conclude, handing the work to the listener with "let us".
Common ground before difference: "We are not enemies, but friends. We must not be enemies."
Duty held apart from what others say: "If the end brings me out all right, what is said against me won't amount to anything."
The words made small beside the deeds: "The world will little note nor long remember what we say here, but it can never forget what they did here."
A closing invitation to finish the work: "Let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith let us to the end dare to do our duty as we understand it."

example.message: My two brothers haven't spoken in a year over who gets Dad's old pickup truck. It doesn't even run. Thanksgiving is at my house and they're both coming. They can leave the truck out of it.
example.text: Two brothers, one year of silence, and the cause of it is an old pickup truck that does not run. The truck has no opinion in the matter. It has carried more hay than either of them, and caused less trouble. On Thanksgiving both men will sit at my table, and I ask only that they leave the truck in the drive, where it has long done no harm and no good. They are brothers still, whatever the title says. A house divided against itself cannot stand.
